content: Amylose, identified by the CAS number 9005-82-7, is a linear polymer composed of glucose molecules primarily connected through α(1→4) glycosidic bonds. This polymer can consist of several thousand glucose units. It is one of the two main components of starch, with the other being amylopectin. The α(1→4) linkages in amylose facilitate the formation of a helical structure. The structural formula of amylose demonstrates its repeating glucose subunits, which can number in the range of 300 to 3000 or more. Compared to amylopectin, amylose is less easily digested by the human body. However, due to its compact structure, it occupies less space, making it a preferred form of carbohydrate storage in plants. Amylose typically constitutes approximately 30% of the starch stored in plants. The enzyme amylase acts on the terminal ends of the amylose molecule, breaking it down into simpler sugars during digestion. A unique property of amylose is its ability to interact with iodine molecules. Iodine fits neatly into the helical structure of amylose, forming a complex that absorbs specific wavelengths of light. This interaction is the basis for a common test for the presence of starch. When a yellow iodine solution is added to a sample containing amylose, a characteristic blue-black color develops. Additionally, rice varieties with high amylose content have been shown to have a significantly lower glycemic load. This property may offer potential benefits for individuals with diabetes, as it could help in better managing blood glucose levels.
